Inordinate
ĭn-ôr´dĭ-nāt
adj. (out of order; excessive; passion loosed from its rule — rendering Greek pathos)
Latin inordinatus, not ordered, from in- (not) and ordinare (to set in order). The word does not mean strong; it means unruled.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Inordinate means out of its appointed order, and the word is exact. Paul commands, “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry” (Col 3:5), and adds the reason: “For which things' sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience” (Col 3:6). The Greek pathos is passion that has slipped its bounds — an affection is not condemned for existing but for ruling where it should serve. Ezekiel uses the word of a nation's spiritual adultery: Aholibah “was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in her whoredoms” (Eze 23:11). John describes the same disorder as the shape of the world itself: “all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world” (1Jn 2:16). This is why Paul ends his list with covetousness, which is idolatry. Inordinate affection is a worship disorder before it is a moral one. Every desire God made has a place and a proportion; when a good thing is loved above its station it becomes a god, and it will exact worship.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines inordinate as irregular; disorderly; excessive; immoderate; not limited to rules prescribed, or to usual bounds.

expand to see more

INOR'DINATE, a. Irregular; disorderly; excessive; immoderate; not limited to rules prescribed, or to usual bounds; as inordinate desires.

2. Not according to order or rule; as an inordinate affection.

INOR'DINATELY, adv. Irregularly; excessively; immoderately.

AFFEC'TION, n. The state of being affected; a bent of mind toward a particular object; passion; love.

Key Scripture

Colossians 3:5 — "Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry:"

Ezekiel 23:11 — "And when her sister Aholibah saw this, she was more corrupt in her inordinate love than she, and in her whoredoms more than her sister in her whoredoms."

Colossians 3:6 — "For which things' sake the wrath of God cometh on the children of disobedience:"

1 John 2:16 — "For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world."

Modern Corruption

Intensity of desire is treated as its own justification, so that a passion strong enough to be called authentic is thereby held to be permitted.

expand to see more

The reigning moral rule of the age is that a desire deeply felt is a desire that must be honoured, and to deny it is to deny the self. Colossians 3:5 answers with a verb: mortify. Paul does not ask whether the affection is sincerely held; he classes inordinate affection with fornication and covetousness and orders it put to death. The word inordinate is precise about the fault. It is not that the desire is intense but that it has left its order — it has taken a place above the God who gave it, and Paul names that place correctly when he calls covetousness idolatry.

The opposite error is the ancient one of treating the affections themselves as the problem, as though the cure for disordered love were less love. Scripture never says so. The remedy for inordinate affection is ordered affection: love God with all the heart, then love the neighbour, then love the wife as Christ loved the church — a hierarchy in which each love is given its proper measure and none is starved. A man is not saved by feeling less; he is saved by loving rightly, and that reordering is the work of the Spirit in sanctification, which is why the command to mortify is addressed to men who are already risen with Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek pathos (G3806), passion, inordinate affection — Colossians 3:5, Romans 1:26, 1 Thessalonians 4:5; epithumia (G1939), strong desire, concupiscence.

expand to see more

Greek pathos (G3806) — passion, inordinate affection; Colossians 3:5, Romans 1:26, 1 Thessalonians 4:5.

Greek epithumia (G1939) — desire, longing, in a bad sense lust; the companion word rendered evil concupiscence.

Greek pleonexia (G4124) — covetousness, the desire for more; Colossians 3:5, identified there with idolatry.

Latin inordinatus — not that the affection is too strong, but that it is out of its order.

Ezekiel 23:11 applies the word to a nation's religion; disordered love is idolatry before it is immorality.

Usage

"“Mortify therefore… inordinate affection” — the command is a verb, not a caution."

"“Covetousness, which is idolatry” — the disorder is a worship disorder."

"The fault is not intensity but station: a good thing loved above its place."
